title: Sheikh Hasina Plans Return to Bangladesh, Dhaka Warns of Immediate Arrest
excerpt: Two years after fleeing a student-led uprising, Bangladesh's ousted former PM says she'll return in December to surrender — but Dhaka says she'll be jailed on arrival.
body:
• Sheikh Hasina told Reuters she plans to return from exile in India around December 2026 with senior Awami League colleagues to surrender in court
  • Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said Hasina will be arrested the moment she enters the country
  • Hasina faces a death sentence from Bangladesh's war-crimes tribunal for ordering a deadly crackdown on student protesters in 2024

Nearly two years after fleeing Bangladesh amid a mass student uprising, ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has declared she will return to face the courts — setting up a high-stakes confrontation with a government that says she'll be arrested the moment she steps on Bangladeshi soil.

In her first interview since going into exile, the 78-year-old told Reuters in July that she and senior members of her banned Awami League party plan to fly back from India around December and surrender.

"They may arrest me on my return, they may even kill me. Still, I have to go. My party leaders and workers are being subjected to tremendous repression. If death comes, I want it to come on my own soil, where my parents are buried and where their blood was shed."

— Sheikh Hasina, in a telephone interview with Reuters

The Road to Exile

Hasina resigned on August 5, 2024, after weeks of student-led protests against a government job quota system escalated into a broader uprising against her 20-year rule. She fled Dhaka by helicopter, landing at India's Hindon Air Force base near New Delhi, where she was received by National Security Advisor Ajit Doval.

The crackdown that preceded her ouster killed as many as 1,400 people, according to a United Nations report. Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was appointed to lead an interim administration, and elections held in February 2026 brought Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's government to power.

In November 2025, Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia on five counts of crimes against humanity, including ordering the use of drones, helicopters, and lethal weapons against civilian protesters. She has denied all charges, calling the proceedings "farcical" and "politically motivated."

Dhaka's Response

Bangladesh's government responded swiftly to Hasina's return announcement. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told reporters in mid-July that there would be no option for a voluntary surrender.

"Sheikh Hasina is a convicted criminal. If she surrenders, action will be taken against her as per the laws of Bangladesh. She will have to go to jail and further proceedings will follow."

— Shama Obaed Islam, Bangladesh State Minister for Foreign Affairs

Obaed dismissed Hasina's statement as "an attempt to mobilise fugitive party leaders and activists." Bangladesh has formally requested India to extradite Hasina and former Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal, who also faces a death sentence. Three ministries have been pursuing the matter since the new government took office in February, according to Reuters.

India's Delicate Position

Hasina's prolonged stay in New Delhi has strained India-Bangladesh ties. India said in April it was examining Bangladesh's extradition request and wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties" — diplomatic language that has satisfied neither side.

For India's large diaspora community, the Bangladesh standoff carries direct implications. Relations between New Delhi and Dhaka affect everything from border security in India's northeastern states to the safety of Hindu minorities in Bangladesh, who make up about 8% of the country's 170 million people. Hasina herself has repeatedly accused the post-ouster governments of enabling violence against minorities.

In January 2026, Hasina delivered her first public address from exile — a pre-recorded audio message played at the Foreign Correspondents' Club in New Delhi, where she called Muhammad Yunus a "murderous fascist" and accused his administration of pushing Bangladesh into "an age of terror." Bangladesh lodged a formal protest with India over the event.

What's Next

Hasina has not disclosed the exact date of her planned return or which court she would appear before, but told Reuters she has held online meetings covering 125 of Bangladesh's 300 parliamentary constituencies as part of efforts to reorganise the Awami League from exile. She said she has not consulted any foreign government on her return plans.

Her return, if it happens, would test Bangladesh's judicial system and force a reckoning with the country's most polarising political figure. It could also ease the diplomatic strain between Dhaka and New Delhi — or inflame it further if India is seen as facilitating her political activities.

The second anniversary of her ouster on August 5 will be closely watched, with Hasina increasingly vocal from exile and Bangladesh's government showing no signs of leniency.
